raw_response:
I've farmed these 7.5 mu for 30 years. I keep 5 mu in wheat-maize rotation and 2.5 mu in cotton. That's what fits my family of two — cotton takes a lot of hand work, especially picking and spraying, so I can't handle too much.

The wheat is already in the ground from last October. Before sowing I put down one 50kg bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base. Now that it's greening up, I'll top-dress with about 20kg of urea per mu at jointing stage — that's what my neighbor Lao Zhang does and his wheat always looks thick and strong. I'll irrigate three times: once now at greening, once at heading, and once at grain filling. My well has enough water. I spray pesticide twice, mainly for aphids and powdery mildew. I use Jimai 22, an improved variety from the seed dealer. Last year I got 460 kg per mu; this year I'm hoping for 480 if the spring doesn't turn too dry.

For summer maize after wheat harvest in early June: I plant hybrid seed, Zhengdan 958 or something similar. I don't plough — there's no time, the growing season is short, and everyone around here plants no-till now. I put one bag of compound fertilizer at planting, then about 15kg urea at big trumpet stage. Two irrigations: one at jointing, one at grain filling. Two pesticide sprays for armyworm and aphids. Should get about 520 kg per mu if the summer rains come.

Cotton on my 2.5 mu: I plough deep in spring because cotton roots need loose soil down deep. I use improved cotton seed, not the old traditional kind that my father used. Base fertilizer is about 60kg compound per mu, plus some urea later when it flowers. Cotton needs careful watering — too much and it grows too tall and drops buds, too little and it wilts. Three irrigations: one at flowering, one at boll setting, one more in August if it's too dry. Pesticide is where cotton really costs me — I spray seven times for bollworm, aphids, and spider mites. It's a lot of money but if I skip even one spray I lose everything. Last year I got 250 kg seed cotton per mu. I'm aiming for 280 this year.

I don't change much from year to year. I watch what my neighbors do. Fertilizer prices went up again, but cutting back is risky — a bad harvest means I can't pay for next year's inputs or my living expenses. I'd rather put a bit too much than too little. That's how I've managed for 30 years.
